opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one that surprised a lot of people, including us at first.

The key intuition is that a rare event isn't governed by rare physics. A once-in-a-century hurricane or an extreme heat wave still obeys the same underlying equations: fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, conservation laws. The event is rare, but the mechanisms that produce it show up constantly in ordinary data. So if your model actually learns the underlying dynamics, rather than memorizing typical outcomes, it can extrapolate to configurations it has rarely or never seen.

That's why architecture matters so much. With neural operators, we're not learning a mapping between fixed-size vectors. We're learning an operator between function spaces, essentially the solution operator of the PDE. It's resolution-invariant and captures multi-scale structure, so it's much closer to learning the physics itself. When the model has the right inductive biases, like respecting symmetries, operating in function space, and capturing long-range interactions through things like Fourier layers, it needs far fewer examples of the extreme case, because the extreme case is built from the same local and global interactions it has learned everywhere else.

The second piece is that you can bring in physics directly. You can add physics-informed losses, where you penalize violations of the governing equations, and you can train on both observational data and simulation data at multiple resolutions. That constraint acts as a powerful regularizer. Even where data is sparse, like in the tails of the distribution, the model can't just do whatever it wants; it has to stay consistent with the physics.

And third, because these models are so fast, sometimes tens of thousands of times faster than traditional numerical solvers, you can generate huge ensembles. For rare events, that's huge. Instead of running fifty ensemble members, you can run thousands and actually sample the tails of the distribution properly. So you're not only predicting the most likely outcome; you're estimating the probability of the extreme one.

Now, I want to be careful here. This isn't magic, and there are real limits. If you're truly outside the regime of the physics you've learned, say a qualitatively new phenomenon, no model is going to save you. That's why validation against physics and uncertainty quantification are so important. But for a lot of the rare events we care about, extreme weather, material failure, turbulence, the rarity is in the outcome, not in the rules. If AI learns the rules, it can handle the rare cases surprisingly well.

r001.rationale: The response says rare events follow the same physical mechanisms as ordinary data and that learning those dynamics lets models generalize to rare configurations.

r002.rationale: It describes AI models learning underlying dynamics and physics, but does not say they uncover structure that traditional numerical methods may miss.

r003.rationale: It notes that traditional solvers are slower, but does not identify correctness across arbitrary scenarios as their priority.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The key is that we're not learning the physics from scratch. When we train a neural operator on something like weather or fluid dynamics, we're learning the solution operator of the underlying partial differential equation, and that operator is shared across all the events, rare and common alike. A hurricane isn't a different physical system from a calm day over the Atlantic. It's the same Navier-Stokes, the same thermodynamics, just in a different regime of the state space. So if the model has genuinely captured the operator rather than memorizing input-output pairs, it generalizes to the tails.

The second piece is resolution invariance. Neural operators learn in function space, not on a fixed grid, so we can train at one resolution and query at another. That lets the model exploit structure that a pixel-based CNN would have to relearn for every scale. Extreme events often involve multiscale interactions, small-scale instabilities feeding into large-scale structures, and having the right inductive bias there matters enormously.

And then honestly there's a data point most people underestimate: the training data is a lot richer than it looks. Forty years of reanalysis at hourly resolution is tens of thousands of global snapshots, and each one contains thousands of local weather patterns. The rare event is rare globally, but the local dynamics that compose it, the sharp gradients, the convective bursts, show up constantly. The model has seen the building blocks many times even if it has only seen a handful of category five storms.

So I'd push back a little on the framing of "few samples." It's few samples of the labeled extreme, but a lot of samples of the physics that generates it, and the architecture is designed to learn the physics.

r001.rationale: The response says rare events share physical dynamics with common events and that their component patterns—such as sharp gradients and convective bursts—appear repeatedly in training data, enabling learning from few labeled extremes.

r002.rationale: It describes learning shared physical operators and multiscale structure, but does not say AI can uncover latent structure that traditional numerical methods may miss.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss traditional numerical methods or identify correctness across arbitrary scenarios as their priority.

astra-6.text:
The key is that rare physical events aren’t governed by a different set of laws. The same underlying dynamics produce both the ordinary behavior and the extremes. So if a model learns those dynamics, it can potentially generalize to events it hasn’t seen many times in training, rather than simply memorizing examples of disasters.

That’s part of the motivation for neural operators: learning mappings between functions, such as how an entire field of pressure or velocity evolves. There’s a lot of structure in those fields, and learning that structure can make models much more data efficient.

But it’s not automatic. A model can do well on average and still miss the extremes. We have to evaluate those events specifically and understand where the model’s predictions become unreliable.

r001.rationale: The response says rare events follow the same underlying dynamics and that learning field structure can improve data efficiency, but it does not identify specific physical signatures as the reason they can be learned from few examples.

r002.rationale: It mentions structure in physical fields, but does not say AI can uncover latent structure in nature that traditional numerical methods may miss.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss traditional numerical methods or identify correctness across arbitrary scenarios as their priority.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that rare physical events are not disconnected from the more common events we observe. They arise from the same underlying dynamics. So if a model learns those dynamics, rather than simply memorizing examples, it can potentially generalize to events it has seen very few times.

Physics also gives us structure: conservation laws, symmetries, and interactions across different scales. Incorporating that structure narrows what the model needs to learn from data. You’re not learning an arbitrary mapping from scratch.

But I would distinguish predicting a rare event from reliably estimating its probability. A model might reproduce an extreme event’s dynamics and still get its frequency wrong. That requires careful validation and uncertainty quantification.

r001.rationale: The response says rare events share underlying dynamics with common events and that learning those dynamics can support generalization from few examples, with physical structure constraining what must be learned.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning underlying dynamics, but does not say AI can uncover latent structure that traditional numerical methods may miss.
